Got it — I won’t change anything. Below is a focused walkthrough of the likely effects of moving a recurring "Board Prep" meeting from the first Tuesday of each month to the second Tuesday of each month in a typical month, and what attendees will see. After this I can (if you want) either check your actual calendar for conflicts or draft an announcement — but I’ll wait for your go-ahead.

High-level summary
- Net effect: every monthly occurrence will shift forward by one week. That can create new conflicts on the second Tuesday, change the lead time relative to related deadlines/meetings, and trigger calendar updates for all attendees.
- What to verify before changing: existing events on second Tuesdays, attendees’ recurring commitments, room/conference availability, any prep deadlines tied to the original first-Tuesday schedule, and time-zone implications.

What this would likely “knock into” in a normal month
- Standing meetings on week 2: any meetings that are scheduled on “the second Tuesday” (committees, leadership syncs, vendor calls, recurring client/board items) would be candidates for conflict.
- Team/department mid-month checkpoints: some groups schedule mid-month reviews or finance/ops check-ins during week 2. Those could overlap.
- Room and conferencing bookings: if you use a shared physical room or a reserved conference bridge, those resources are more likely to be booked on the second Tuesday.
- Prep deadlines and review cadence: if people rely on the first-Tuesday slot as a buffer before the board meeting or monthly reporting deadlines, shifting to week 2 may shorten or change that buffer. Conversely, it could increase the buffer if the board meeting is later in the month — check what the board meeting date is relative to prep.
- Payroll/finance or compliance deadlines: some organizations have recurring mid-month operational deadlines that fall near week 2. These are less likely but worth checking if your organization uses a mid-month schedule.
- Recurrence exceptions: if there are already exceptions or single-instance events on specific months (e.g., holiday overrides), moving the series can interact awkwardly with those exceptions and produce duplicate or missing occurrences in some calendar systems.

What attendees will see (typical calendar systems: Outlook/Gmail)
- A calendar update notification: attendees will receive an “Updated event” invite for the series (or for future occurrences, depending on how you edit it). The update usually includes the new date for each occurrence.
- Old event removed / new event added (or duplicates if handled incorrectly): if you update the whole series, their calendars will replace the first-Tuesday entries with second-Tuesday entries. If you change individual occurrences instead of the series, some attendees may see both the original and the new instance (duplicates) or an exception.
- RSVP status: their prior RSVPs may remain but some systems mark the event as “Needs response” after a date/time change — attendees may need to re-accept.
- Conflicts flagged on attendees’ calendars: those who already have commitments at the new time will see a conflict or double-booking. They may receive no automatic resolution — they must decline or reschedule.
- Meeting room / conferencing changes: if the event uses a room resource or reserved conference link that is already booked on the second Tuesday, the resource booking may fail or quietly be removed, depending on the calendar system; attendees will see the meeting without the room if that happens.
- Time-zone impact: attendees in different time zones will see the meeting shifted accordingly; if the shift crosses a daylight saving boundary in some regions but not others, that can produce unexpected local-time changes.
- Notifications and agenda views: in day/week/month calendar views the event will appear on the second Tuesday. Attendees who view a weekly agenda will see the event one week later in the month; folks relying on automatic reminders may get them at different points relative to their other tasks.

Edge cases and gotchas
- Series exceptions: if there are past exceptions (canceled or moved occurrences) in the series, editing the series may produce odd results; some calendar systems create exceptions rather than fully replacing entries.
- One-off attendees / permissions: if the meeting includes external guests who were only invited to certain occurrences, confirm whether you want the change to apply to all occurrences and guests.
- Shared calendar syncing delays: large organizations sometimes have propagation delays; some recipients may not see updates immediately.
- Duplicate conferencing links: if your system creates a new conferencing link for the changed series, attendees may have two links (old vs new) in messages unless you explicitly keep the same link.

Practical checklist to run before making the change (recommended)
1. Scan second-Tuesday occurrences for: recurring team meetings, committee meetings, all-hands, finance/ops checkpoints, and room/conference bookings.
2. Check the board meeting date and any downstream deadlines (reports, slide decks, approvals) to confirm the prep window remains adequate.
3. Verify key attendees’ fixed commitments (executives, chairs) on second Tuesdays.
4. Confirm room and conferencing availability for the new date/time.
5. Decide whether to update the entire series or only future occurrences (and be aware of exception behavior).
6. Draft a short notice to attendees explaining the reason, the timing, and asking them to confirm conflicts or propose alternatives.
7. If external attendees exist, call out time-zone changes explicitly in the notice.

Would you like me to:
- Check your actual calendar for conflicts (I can if you give me permission), or
- Run a hypothetical “normal month” example with a sample weekly schedule to show typical collisions, or
- Draft an announcement/notification to send to attendees when you’re ready?

Tell me which next step you want; I’ll wait for your go-ahead.
